name: Bee venom face mask

card.summary: A skincare mask or cream containing bee venom (apitoxin), marketed as a natural alternative to Botox for a smoother, plumper, firmer-looking face.
card.aka: Bee venom skincare; apitoxin mask; faux-tox
card.note: Bee venom is a known allergen; people with bee or wasp sting allergy are generally advised by manufacturers and allergists to avoid it.

quick.overview:
Bee venom face masks and creams contain apitoxin, the venom honeybees use for defense, or a synthetic or purified version of its components such as melittin. Brands, especially in Korean and other cosmeceutical lines, market them as a "natural Botox" for tightening, smoothing and plumping the look of the skin.

Marketing explains the effect through mild tingling and a gentle inflammatory or circulation-boosting response in the skin. Published literature describes bee venom's biological activities and its place among bee products in dermatology and Korean cosmeceuticals, while controlled human trials of cosmetic bee venom masks for wrinkles are not found in the research record.
quick.how: Users apply the cream or sheet mask to clean skin for a set time, often as part of a multi-step routine, and may repeat it weekly or more often depending on the product. Some also try creams under the eyes, hoping for firmer-looking skin; forum discussion of that use is mixed.
quick.risks: Bee venom contains allergenic proteins, and products can cause local irritation, redness, swelling and stinging. People with known bee or wasp sting allergy are usually advised to avoid venom-containing products. Patch testing is commonly recommended by brands. Under-eye skin is thin, which forum users note as a concern.

lead: A bee venom face mask is a topical skincare product containing bee venom (apitoxin) or its isolated components, sold for a smoother, firmer and brighter look. It belongs to the family of animal-derived ingredients used in Korean cosmetics, alongside snail mucin and synthetic snake-venom peptides [3]. Marketing often calls it "faux-tox" or a natural alternative to botulinum toxin.

Bee venom is a mixture whose main peptide is melittin, with smaller amounts of apamin, the enzyme phospholipase A2, hyaluronidase and histamine; phospholipase A2 is one of its principal allergens [12]. Review articles describe anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial and other biological activities for venom and its fractions, mostly in laboratory and animal work, and discuss venom-containing market products [1]. A review of bee products in dermatology and skin care covers venom together with honey, propolis and royal jelly as ingredients for skin treatment and care [2].

No randomized trial of a cosmetic bee venom mask for wrinkles appears in the research record. Human trials of bee venom exist for other purposes, such as allergen immunotherapy, neck pain, Parkinson's disease and temporomandibular muscle pain with topical application [4][5][9].

chain: Bee venom applied in a mask or cream
Skin experiences mild tingling and a local response
Product claims smoother, plumper, firmer-looking skin
angle.text: Users apply the product hoping for a lifted, smoother look similar to what injectables give. Brands attribute this to a gentle skin response to venom components; the claim is made by marketing rather than shown in published cosmetic trials.

paras: Honeybee venom is composed mainly of melittin (about half of the venom peptides), apamin (about 2%), phospholipase A2 (about 12%), hyaluronidase and histamine. Phospholipase breaks down cell membranes and hyaluronidase widens vessels and spreads the venom through tissue; the venom is known to cause local inflammation [12].
Cosmetic products may use whole venom, purified fractions or synthetic peptides, and concentrations vary by brand.

Bee venom is promoted for firming, smoothing and brightening, often in sheet masks and creams from K-beauty brands. A review of ingredients in Korean cosmeceuticals lists bee venom among animal-derived actives with reported biological activities relevant to skin rejuvenation, and calls for further research [3].

On looksmax.org, one user proposed using bee venom cream under the eyes on the theory that venom-induced dilation and fluid movement might change under-eye appearance, while also worrying about repeated low-grade inflammation in thin skin. A reply argued that vessel dilation would not address a lack of infraorbital support, and another asked to see before and after examples [11].

No studies found on bee venom face masks for facial appearance. Related research includes reviews of bee venom pharmacology [1][6], bee products in dermatology [2], a randomized trial of bee venom acupuncture with NSAIDs for neck pain [4], a trial in Parkinson's disease [5], and a registered trial of topical bee venom for jaw muscle pain [9]. A registered trial compared local allergic responses to two bee venom pharmacopuncture preparations in healthy volunteers [7].

Allergists treat bee venom as a major allergen, and venom immunotherapy is a medical treatment with its own trials [8]. Cosmetic labels typically advise against use in people allergic to bee stings and advise avoiding contact with the eyes. A US over-the-counter wart and corn product containing bee venom carries a label for external use only and says to avoid the face [FDA].

lore.intro: Bee venom skincare appears in forum discussion as a possible way to firm or de-puff skin, including under the eyes [11].

claims.claim: Bee venom cream can act like a natural Botox
claims.believers: Brands and users say mild venom-induced stinging and circulation increases leave skin smoother and plumper.
claims.experts: Reviews describe venom's biological activities and its use in Korean cosmeceuticals, and say more research is needed [3]; no published trial tests facial wrinkle outcomes.

claims.claim: Bee venom cream could help puffy under-eyes
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster reasoned that venom increases circulation and fluid movement under the skin [11].
claims.experts: Other forum members replied that vessel dilation does not provide infraorbital support [11]; no studies test this use.
